The '''Denver Contract Detention Facility''', also known as the '''Aurora ICE Processing Center,'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-12 |title=Results of an Unannounced Inspection of ICE's Denver Contract Detention Facility in Aurora, Colorado |url=https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2024-06/OIG-24-29-Jun24.pdf |location=Washington, DC |website=Department of Homeland Security}}</ref> is a privately run [[immigration detention center]] located in [[Aurora, Colorado]]. It is operated by the [[GEO Group]], a private prison corporation, under contract from [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|US Immigration and Customs Enforcement]]. Its capacity was increased from 1,360 to 1,530 in late 2025.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Toomer |first=Lindsey |date=January 12, 2026 |title=Aurora ICE facility population near capacity after recent expansion |url=https://coloradonewsline.com/briefs/aurora-ice-population-capacity/ |access-date=2026-03-27 |website=Colorado Newsline |language=en-US}}</ref> It is the only major ICE detention facility in Colorado.<ref name=":1" />

US Congressman Jason Crow was denied entry for an inspection visit to the facility in January 2026.<ref name=":1" />

== History ==
The [[Wackenhut Corrections Corporation]] (later renamed The GEO Group), established in 1984, received its first contract for an immigration detention facility to operate the Aurora-based facility in 1987.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Towle |first=Sarah |title=Crossing the Line (Revised Edition): Finding America in the Borderlands |date=2025-09-30 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=979-8-89636-135-0}}</ref> The facility was built in 150 days.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1988-12-05 |title=PRIVATE COMPANIES LOCK INTO PRISON BUSINESS WACKENHUT NABS CONTRACT TO BUILD, OPERATE DETENTION CENTER IN TEXAS |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/1988/12/05/private-companies-lock-into-prison-business-wackenhut-nabs-contract-to-build-operate-detention-center-in-texas/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Sun Sentinel |language=en-US}}</ref>

In July 2026, an employee, who was leaving the facility, shot a protestor in the foot with his personal firearm during a confrontation.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Liederman |first=Mack |last2=MacDonald |first2=John S. W. |date=2026-07-24 |title=ICE Contractor Faces Charges in Shooting Outside Colorado Detention Center |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/23/us/colorado-ice-protest-shooting-geo-group.html |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The employee faces charges including attempted second-degree murder.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Slevin |first=Colleen |date=2026-07-17 |title=Aurora ICE detention center worker arrested in shooting of protester |url=https://coloradosun.com/2026/07/17/aurora-ice-detention-center-worker-arrested-in-connection-with-shooting-of-protester/ |access-date=2026-08-01 |work=Colorado Sun}}</ref> 

== Layout ==
The facility includes one large detention "North" building and a smaller annex (subdivided into East and West), connected by a covered walkway. Male detainees are housed in both the North and Annex buildings; female and transgender detainees are in separate housing units in the Annex.<ref name=":0" />

== Deaths in detention and detainee treatment ==
As of 2022, there had been three deaths of detainees at the facility.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-10-14 |title=Archived: Nicaraguan man in ICE custody passes away at Colorado hospital {{!}} ICE |url=https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/nicaraguan-man-ice-custody-passes-away-colorado-hospital |access-date=2026-04-01}}</ref>

In 2017, 64-year-old detainee Kamyar Samimi died after two weeks in the Aurora detention facility. Samimi had been receiving [[methadone]] treatment for two decades to manage his opioid addiction, but was denied access to the drug once detained.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last= |date=2023-08-30 |title=ICE records reveal more information about 2017, 2022 deaths inside Aurora detention facility |url=https://www.cpr.org/2023/08/30/npr-investigation-ice-aurora-facility-deaths-colorado/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Colorado Public Radio |language=en}}</ref> According to a review of records by Colorado Public Radio, as Samimi underwent withdrawal, medical staff in the facility skipped multiple medical checks on him and "used a withdrawal protocol for alcohol — not opioids."<ref name=":2" /> The American Civil Liberties Union filed a wrongful death lawsuit in September 2019 in his case.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ACLU of Colorado Sues GEO for the Wrongful Death of Kamyar Samimi |url=https://www.aclu-co.org/press-releases/aclu-colorado-sues-geo-wrongful-death-kamyar-samimi/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=ACLU of Colorado |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-11-12 |title=ACLU of Colorado sues prison company over death at Aurora ICE detention facility |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2019/11/12/aclu-colorado-lawsuit-aurora-ice-samimi-death/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=The Denver Post |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2022, 39-year-old detainee Melvin Ariel Calero Mendoza died of a pulmonary embolism while detained at the Aurora facility.<ref name=":2" /> Records showed that Calero-Mendoza "had been complaining for weeks about pain and swelling in his leg." In a 911 call after the prisoner collapsed, a facility employee failed to share specifics on the man's medical condition, misstated the facility access and put the 911 dispatcher on hold.<ref name=":2" /> An attorney for the family stated, "The depth of indifference that this caller displayed was shocking. The family is disappointed and horrified by this call."<ref name=":2" /> 

In March 2026, a coalition of groups, including the American Friends Service Committee, issued a report on conditions in the Aurora facility based on the testimony of 31 detainees. The report alleged neglect of physical and mental health conditions, malnutrition, extreme temperatures, physical and emotional abuse, and forced labor. The GEO Group denied the accusations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harris |first=Kyle |date=2026-03-02 |title=Aurora ICE detainees are malnourished and forced to work, advocates report |url=https://denverite.com/2026/03/02/aurora-geo-immigration-jail-ice-conditions-report/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |work=Denverite}}</ref>

In July 2026, the Aurora City Council demanded that The GEO Group cooperate with the city's investigation into a case of tuberculosis at the detention center.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Daley |first=John |date=2026-07-28 |title=Aurora warns of legal consequences for GEO Group, without cooperation on TB investigation at crowded immigration detention center |url=https://www.cpr.org/2026/07/28/tuberculosis-geo-ice-facility-aurora-investigation/ |access-date=2026-08-01 |work=Colorado Public Radio}}</ref>
